o: Lord God, I thank You for this dawn and for the life You grant me. Before the day claims me with its tasks, I want to stop before You and acknowledge that You are the foundation of all that I am. Thank You for Your Word, which is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path, and for Your Son Jesus Christ, who is the firm rock on which I can lean.

I pray that today I may build my life on Your teachings. May I not be content merely to hear them, but put them into practice in my home, in my work and in my relationships. When the rains, the floods and the winds of trial come, may I not be afraid, for my house is founded on You. Be my refuge and my strength, my ever-present help in trouble.

Thank You, for Your Church has only one head, who is Christ. Bless all who serve You in every place, the pastors, the teachers and the simple brothers and sisters who pray in silence. Give me the humility not to place my trust in men, but in You. Guide me by Your Spirit, give me wisdom and peace, and help me be a reflection of Your love throughout this day. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 3, 1534, the Parliament of England passed the Act of Supremacy. It declared that King Henry VIII was the supreme head of the Church of England, thereby breaking the authority the pope had until then exercised over the Church in that kingdom. It is a very well-documented fact that marked a profound turning point in the religious history of England.

This act had great consequences. It changed the way the Church was governed in the kingdom and opened the door for the Bible, in the following years, to circulate in the English language with more freedom. For many ordinary people, this meant being able to hear the Word of God in the language they spoke at home, without depending on another language they did not understand.

But history also leaves us a delicate lesson. Kings and authorities pass away, their decisions are debated and, over time, evaluated in different ways. What the Scriptures teach with clarity is that the true head of the Church is no human ruler, but Jesus Christ himself. This is what the apostle Paul affirms when he writes that Christ is the head of the body, the Church.

Jesus, at the end of the Sermon on the Mount, said that whoever hears his words and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. The rain fell, the floods came, the winds blew, and the house did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. The events of nations change, but the Word of Christ remains firm for the one who decides to build on it. Therefore, in remembering this date, we give thanks for the Word we can read today, and we look to Christ as the Lord to whom his Church belongs.
m.c: Go out into this day with the assurance that Christ is the rock that does not move. May his peace be your shelter, his Word your guide and his presence your strength. Walk with confidence: the one who sustains you is greater than any storm.
m: It is easy to trust in what we can see: a position, an institution, a strong person or a well-laid plan. But history shows us that all of this can change from one year to the next. When we remember events like the Act of Supremacy of 1534, we see how human events move history forward, and we also understand that we need a foundation that does not depend on them.

Jesus expressed it with a simple image: two houses, two foundations. The difference was not that one withstood the storm and the other did not experience it. Both received the same rain, the same wind and the same floods. The difference was in the foundation. The one who heard and obeyed built on the rock. The one who heard and did not obey built on the sand.

Today you can do something concrete. Think of an area of your life where you have trusted more in your own strength or in people than in God: your finances, your health, your family or your work. Bring that area to prayer and ask the Lord which word of his you should obey there. Perhaps it is forgiving someone, speaking truthfully, being patient or taking a first step you have put off. Obeying is laying one brick on the rock.

And when fear knocks at your door, remember the words of the psalmist: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear.” Christ is the head of his Church and the Lord of your life. As long as you are united to him, no storm will have the last word. Build today with care, with humility and with obedience, and you will see that your house stands firm.

o: Good Father, at nightfall I want to thank You for every moment of this day. Thank You for the health You gave me, for the food on the table, for the people who smiled at me and also for those who taught me something hard. Everything I lived today happened under Your gaze, and I know that nothing escaped You. I thank You because You are a God who is near.

Lord Jesus, just as You entered Simon's house and drew near to a woman sick in bed, today come into every corner of my life that needs Your touch. Take my hand where I am weak and lift me up. Heal what is weary in my body, in my mind and in my heart. Give me a grateful spirit that, once raised up, knows how to serve You with joy.

I give You my burdens from this day, my unsettled matters and the people I love who are sick or sad today. Turn my mourning into dancing, undo my sackcloth and clothe me with joy, so that my soul may sing to You and not be silent. May I rest tonight in Your peace, and may I rise tomorrow with new strength to serve others with love. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: The Gospel of Mark tells us that as Jesus left the synagogue in Capernaum, he went with James and John to the house of Simon and Andrew. There they found an unexpected problem: Simon's mother-in-law was in bed with a fever. It was not a moment of great crowds or speeches; it was a simple need, inside a home, on a day of rest.

The disciples told him about her at once. It is beautiful to notice that they did not wait for the situation to get worse, nor did they hesitate to tell Jesus what was happening. They placed the need before the Master, and the text says he came to her, took her by the hand and lifted her up. No long ritual was needed: a gesture of tenderness and power was enough.

Mark adds a brief and touching detail: “And the fever left her, and she began to serve them.” The healing was complete and swift. This woman did not stay thinking about herself, but, once restored, she began to serve those who were in her home. Her gratitude turned into action, in the simple service of welcoming guests.

That same evening, according to the account, at sundown many sick people were brought to the door of the house, and Jesus healed many of them. It all began in a home, with a hand reaching out to someone who could not get up by herself. The story teaches us that the Lord cares about the small and the everyday, and that his hand, always outstretched, lifts up and restores strength to serve. And that same hand remains outstretched today toward those who feel powerless and need a touch of his grace.
t.c: May the Lord take your hand tonight as he took that woman's, and lift you up by his peace. Give him what has weighed on you today and sleep quietly. Tomorrow, his goodness will find you again, ready to renew your strength.
m: At the end of a day, you may feel that you are at the end of your strength, like someone who has been in bed for hours with a fever. It may not be a physical illness; it may be a weariness of the soul, a worry that will not leave or a sadness you do not know how to name. The story of Peter's mother-in-law invites us to remember that we can bring this condition directly to Jesus.

Observe what the disciples did: they spoke to Jesus about her. They did not try to fix everything themselves. Tonight you can do the same. Speak before the Lord the names of the people you love who are going through a hard time, and tell him also how you yourself feel. Simple, sincere and trusting prayer is the way we place needs in his hands.

Then notice how the story ends: “and she began to serve them.” God's healing is not only relief for us; it is also the door to grateful service. Before sleeping, think of a simple way to serve tomorrow: making breakfast for your family, calling someone who is alone, offering your help at work or simply listening with patience. Gratitude becomes visible when it turns into service.

Remember the words of the psalmist: “You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness.” God is able to transform your heavy nights into bright mornings. You do not have to settle everything tonight. Put your hand in his, close your eyes and rest. When morning comes, he will lift you up again, with strength to love and to serve.
